video_title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data — Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
gist: Latent Space interviews Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, on building a legal agent platform when the company cannot see customer data: tabular review, lists and agent primitives, eval heat maps where model releases both improve and regress tasks, model arbitrage plus narrow post-training, Azure-first privacy, forward-deployed and legal engineers, and what AI does to law firm economics (junior roles, billing, partnership). Tone is bullish that depth in vertical agents beats frontier labs' breadth.

insights.claim: Legora started as a ChatGPT-style search tool over Swedish law, then evolved into an agent that drafts, edits Word files, organizes files and runs complex analyses; the assistant-to-agent switch happened roughly a year before the interview, around the Sonnet/Opus 4.6 generation of models.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Agent-lab products emerge from simple wrappers once model capability crosses thresholds.

insights.claim: Tabular review fans one question per column across thousands of documents (one row per document, scaling to about a million cells), with citations back to source, cell-level comments, and a test-on-first-10-rows step; the agent can spin one up itself when given 10,000 files.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Spreadsheet-style fan-out is the sticky form factor for due diligence and extraction.
insights.quote: People are happy to live there.

insights.claim: Legora builds on a few reusable primitives (lists like a Notion database/Linear, projects of files, the agent, tabular review) so legal engineers can compose new products, such as fund dashboards, and agents can create and read lists; the acquired Wexler fact-intelligence product was built on the same primitives.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Primitive-based architecture lets a small engineering team ship many verticalized products.
insights.quote: how do we build a core primitive that we can scale to to many different end products

insights.claim: Intake is a legal-specific Slack front door that creates tasks in a list, kicks off agents, and returns finished work to Slack so the legal team can manage agents inside Legora.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Workflow orchestration (not just doing the work) is the expanding product surface.

insights.claim: Legora has an unreleased idea of letting the agent be the API (trigger the agent instead of calling endpoints), constrained by unbounded cost, latency and nondeterminism, with roughly two in a hundred runs doing something unwanted.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Agents as interfaces could replace some API surface if reliability improves.

insights.claim: Legora only started offering APIs about six months before the interview, having resisted to avoid maintaining old versions while moving fast with about 20 engineers; the team is now about 100 engineers and feels too small.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Platform/API obligations become affordable only after scale.
insights.quote: we're 100 engineers now and it's just like we're way too small

insights.claim: Legora tracks every model across practice areas and tasks in a heat map; model releases often improve some areas while regressing others, more often than expected, and the eval team is about three engineers and three lawyers drawing on a pool of ex-big-law 'legal engineers'.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Task-level eval infrastructure is the moat when model releases are non-monotonic.

insights.claim: A citation-accuracy problem went from about 70% to 99% with a single model release without Legora doing anything, which is why evals were deprioritized in favor of harness building until recently.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Model upgrades erase application-layer bug work, favoring thin scaffolding.
insights.quote: It went from like 70% to like 99.

insights.claim: Legora estimates models can already do roughly 60% of legal work well, with the rest a power distribution of complex analysis needing more intelligence, and much legal work does not need top-tier (Mythos-level) models; users nonetheless demanded a model picker, which Legora resisted and then added.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Cost and latency, not intelligence, are the next constraint for most legal tasks.
insights.quote: a lot of legal work does not require Mythos level intelligence

insights.claim: Legora does model arbitrage: frontier models for the main agent, specific models for sub-tasks (older Gemini and Microsoft's transcription model for speech-to-text and speaker attribution), and open-weight models post-trained only for bounded tasks like legal research retrieval rather than competing on a main agent model.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Application companies capture value by routing and narrow post-training, not frontier training.
insights.quote: We're not trying to like train our own Fable.

insights.claim: Frontier models are too chatty for contract drafting; Astra is cited as concise, and Legora expects the next Anthropic model to do better.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Verbosity is a live differentiator for professional-writing use cases.

insights.claim: Sub-agent delegation for fan-out retrieval, once hard, now works very well; long-document reasoning with edits across a huge contract (definition and ordering consistency) remains hard, and Legora has swung between map-reduce and chunking as models improve.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Scaffolding must be rewritten every model generation.

insights.claim: Defaults in retrieval leave value on the table: do not take default embeddings, customize them (Voyage was mentioned), but ensure multilingual support; Legora's search engineer pushed Turbopuffer toward multi-vector support.
insights.speaker: Host (Latent Space)
insights.so_what: Domain-tuned embeddings are an under-used edge in RAG-heavy products.

insights.claim: Legora cannot view traces or customer data because it is confidential and often belongs to law firms' clients, so it relies on online evals, classification into failure modes and practice areas, and anonymization-by-request to approximate usage.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Regulated-vertical AI vendors operate without usage visibility, slowing iteration.
insights.quote: we can't look at any traces basically

insights.claim: Early law-firm buyers insisted on Azure because Microsoft 365 was already security-reviewed; Amazon and Google were distrusted, on-prem demands have disappeared, and the data processing agreement is kept to very few vendors (hence no ElevenLabs).
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Microsoft's incumbency eased cloud adoption in legal; vendor sprawl is a procurement risk.

insights.claim: Buying a law firm would yield real inputs but not clear outputs, and may raise client-data ownership problems, so real user traces are far more valuable than acquired end products.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Data-acquisition shortcuts in legal are weaker than live product traces.

insights.claim: The partnership model exists because human capital is the only capital professional firms have; Legora wants to help firms codify their way of working into durable IP (e.g., a self-improving knowledge graph), but current eat-what-you-kill partner incentives discourage building shared assets.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Firms that solve the incentive problem for codified assets could change law-firm economics.

insights.claim: Rather than eliminating juniors, AI polarizes: good junior lawyers and engineers are worth more because they produce much more, while pure document-grind tasks are automated; a 'meat proxy' role is replaced by AI-fluent legal engineers.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Entry-level headcount demand shifts toward tool-fluent talent rather than disappearing.
insights.quote: Paralegals gone, yep. Junior lawyers gone, I don't need them.

insights.claim: Billing is moving from hours toward project fees for lower-end work, some of it done for free, with money remaining in strategic work such as M&A and litigation, while freed time goes to client relationships that firms previously did uncompensated.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Hourly billing erodes at the low end while high-value work retains pricing power.

insights.claim: Lawyers adopt AI despite hourly incentives because they understand competitive pressure on their business model is high; the Legora CTO's earlier view had been that legal tech would fail because efficiency lowers earnings.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Adoption is driven by competitive fear, not efficiency gains alone.

insights.claim: American law firms and corporates move faster, treat AI as strategic, and want heavy custom builds (CRM, DMS integrations, triggers) while European ones lean toward off-the-shelf products and product feedback.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Custom-integration demand shapes how much services capacity US growth requires.

insights.claim: Legora uses forward-deployed engineers (first hired about nine months earlier, a YC founder) alongside non-coding legal engineers: legal engineers configure the product like power users, FDEs write production integration code, and the model is expected to evolve to rotating FDE groups placed at clients for about two months.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Palantir-style services layers are reappearing in vertical AI.

insights.claim: Legora's CTO believes law firms will mostly use Legora directly while large enterprises may call it through Claude Cowork-style tools; labs will go broad but not deep in legal, and a $400 million M&A deal will use Legora rather than a general assistant.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: The agent-lab thesis assumes depth beats lab breadth in high-stakes verticals.
insights.quote: if you're doing a you know, $400 million M&A transaction you're going to want Legora.

insights.claim: Legora's strategic bets that customers did not ask for, namely the agent and in-product collaboration, were what moved the product; most roadmap items come from a mountain of customer demand.
insights.speaker: Jacob Lauritzen (CTO, Legora)
insights.so_what: Leading customers on agency, rather than following requests, paid off.
